prayer.text: Saint Peter Julian Eymard, pray for us.

cues.text: A Vow Made in Illness
Born in 1811 at La Mure, in the French Alps, Peter Julian was raised by a mother whose own devotion instilled in him an early love for the Blessed Sacrament.
As a young novice, he was reduced to the point of death by serious illness.
He prayed for the grace to live long enough to say a single Mass and recovered—a moment he later understood as the beginning of his priestly vocation.
He was ordained for the Diocese of Grenoble in 1834.
A Eucharistic Experience

While carrying the Blessed Sacrament in procession at a church in Lyons on the feast of Corpus Christi in 1845, Peter Julian experienced an intense spiritual attraction to Christ's Eucharistic presence.
This reshaped the entire direction of his priestly life, resolving from that point onward to 'preach nothing but Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ Eucharistic.'
From the Marists to a New Congregation

Peter Julian had joined the Marist Fathers in 1839, but when his request to write a specifically Eucharistic rule for a lay association was declined as outside the Marist charism, he sought and received permission to leave the order.
In May 1856, he founded a new religious community in Paris, the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament (Blessed Sacrament Fathers), devoted expressly to promoting Eucharistic adoration.
Reviving Frequent Communion

Working against a lingering Jansenist-influenced culture that discouraged frequent reception of Communion, Peter Julian's new congregation reached out particularly to non-practicing Catholics and to adults whose religious formation had been neglected in childhood, preparing them to return to the sacraments.
Two years later, with Marguerite Guillot, he founded a corresponding community of women, the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament.
A Life of Sustained Opposition
Peter Julian's new foundation faced years of institutional obstacles, financial hardship, and slow, uncertain growth.
It finally secured full ecclesiastical approval.
He himself once described his difficult labors as fertilizer laid at the base of a tree whose fruit he would not live to see.
Legacy
Peter Julian died at La Mure in 1868, only three years after being elected superior general for life of the congregation he had founded.
Canonized in 1962 by Pope John XXIII , just one day after the close of the first session of the Second Vatican Council , he is remembered as the Apostle of the Eucharist.
His two religious communities carried forward, well beyond his own lifetime, the revival of Eucharistic devotion he had begun almost alone.
